blocks.text: Keller Synth (from German Keller, meaning "cellar" or "basement") or Tänzelcore (from German tänzeln, meaning "to prance") are two names for the same underground electronic music subgenre, both coined by the artist Sigfrid in the late 2010s. The genre fuses the eerie medieval themes of Dungeon Synth with the raw aggression of Black Metal and intentionally lo-fi, unpolished production.

Musically, Keller Synth is characterized by frenetic drum programming, lo-fi production techniques, and synth work that blends medieval tonalities with aggressive textures. Black metal elements, including shrieked vocals and distorted guitar passages or synthesizer mimicry of black metal composition, are frequently incorporated. The production deliberately retains recording imperfections including warble, tape hiss, room noise, and distortion.

Aesthetically, the genre employs high-contrast color schemes of neon green and black, featuring imagery such as woodcut-style figures, dancing witches/gnomes, and other medieval or fantastical subjects rendered in deliberately crude or amateurish styles.

Originally an obscure subgenre with roots in Saarland region of Germany, Keller Synth gained wider recognition through social media platforms including TikTok and YouTube in the early 2020s, where the genre's recognizable aesthetic became became a meme. Notable artists associated with the genre's development and popularization include Sigfrid, Andreas Bettinger (as a precursor/influence), Hexenmeister, Tenebris, and Opiated Devilsperm.
History
Origins and Influences

Keller Synth's origins are rooted in the Black Metal scene of Saarland, Germany during the late 1990s and early 2000s. The region was experiencing significant industrial and economic decline following the closure of its historical coal mines and steel mills, creating an environment of rural isolation that directly shaped the scene's development. Unable to afford expensive studio time or traditional instruments, local musicians retreated into the basements (Keller) of cheap housing.

Andreas "B.S.o.D." Bettinger (born August 1, 1980) pioneered the genre's sound by fusing Dungeon Synth atmospheres with gritty black metal electronics and cheap drum machines instead of guitars. His work established the genre's sonic template and thematic focus on severe substance abuse. Bettinger's public musical output and stated ideology romanticize heroin use, most directly in his Keller Synth side project Heroin Macht Glücklich (Heroin Makes Happy). His late wife Sandra contributed through the project Blod Besvimelse, whose 1999 track "Misanthrop" later became associated with the "Crawly the Gnome" TikTok trend.
Formalization and Popularization

Justin Reiter (Sigfrid, born 2002) expanded the style and formally named it "Keller Synth" in 2018, establishing the genre and its visual aesthetic through multiple projects including Grollfried, Friedhof, Schändermond, and Bergënot. His project Bergënot incorporated elements of Hard Techno, Gabber, and Speedcore, coining the related genre "Tänzelcore"; though the two names are largely used synonymously by listeners, some fans draw a distinction where Keller Synth stays truer to its dungeon synth roots while Tänzelcore emphasizes the rave and hardcore elements.

Initially confined to German underground circles on Bandcamp and RateYourMusic, Keller Synth transitioned into a global internet phenomenon during the early-to-mid 2020s via TikTok and YouTube. The genre's expansion was driven by the juxtaposition of distorted medievalism and "raving wizard" imagery, which resonated with internet irony culture. This visibility triggered an influx of Generation Z producers establishing active projects in Indonesia (Tenebris), Brazil (Dementar), and Eastern Europe (Hexenmeister in Donetsk, Warlock Corpse in Kazakhstan), who frequently integrate regional folklore into the genre's thematic elements.
Visuals

Keller Synth and Tänzelcore relies heavily on digital distortion and crudeness, frequently referred to as "shitty medievalism." It is primarily identified by a high-saturation neon green (or purple) on black color palette, resulting in images that resemble "deep-fried" early computer graphics or low-resolution bitmaps.

A central motif is the "Cocky Wizard" or "Prancing Wizard," which consists of classical woodcut illustrations digitally manipulated to appear as if they are dancing or raving. A specific recurring gesture is the "Nose Thumb," a traditional sign of mockery where a thumb is placed to the nose with wiggling fingers. This imagery is deeply rooted in Germanic trickster folklore, referencing figures like Till Eulenspiegel. This sign is often edited onto characters in album art to signal the genre's mischievous attitude.

Other common visual elements include the Triskelion, a three-legged sun face symbol often featured in lime green, and Amanita muscaria mushrooms. While mushrooms are depicted to reference foraging, the aesthetic is heavily tied to the romanticization of hard drug use. Reflecting the themes of B.S.o.D. projects like Heroin Makes Happy, the visual atmosphere frequently incorporates imagery of damp basements, ruins, and obscure rural German landscapes filtered to look alien and toxic, hinting at severe substance abuse. Typography typically involves illegible black metal logos mixed with crude, pixelated medieval fonts.

Another prominent mascot within the scene is the Blemmyae, a mythological headless humanoid with its face located on its torso. This figure gained recognition after appearing on the cover of an early split album between Corneus and Grollfried (projects operated by Bettinger and Sigfrid, respectively), representing a bridge between the genre's two founding figures.

In video formats, such as looping background media and music videos, artists frequently apply a continuous hue-shifting effect to these static graphics. This technique cycles the image through the entire neon color spectrum over time, which is then paired with extreme contrast and digital bitcrushing to maintain the genre's degraded, low-resolution aesthetic.
Typography and Logos
Keller Synth features a highly distinct approach to typography that parodies traditional Black Metal aesthetics.

Band logos are intentionally crude, often appearing hand-drawn in MS Paint or sketched with deliberate sloppiness. These logos prioritize extreme illegibility, utilizing chaotic, squiggly linework that integrates esoteric symbols directly into the lettering, such as inverted crosses, pentagrams, wizard hats, and crescent moons.

Online, such as in adherents' usernames, track listings, and playlist titles (e.g., Sigfrid's official 𖤐⛈𓉢𝔗𝑎̈𝑛𝑧𝑒𝑙𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒𓉢⛈𖤐🂠 Spotify playlist), this aesthetic translates into the heavy use of Unicode symbols, ASCII art, and Fraktur (medieval) text generators to create cluttered, heavily stylized text strings (e.g., 𝔗𝔞̈𝔫𝔷𝔢𝔩𝔠𝔬𝔯𝔢).
Fashion

Due to its internet-first nature, Keller Synth and Tänzelcore's aesthetic primarily manifests through cassette layouts, album art, and social media fan profiles rather than everyday dress. However, on TikTok, some participants combine pointed witch hats with outdoor wear, sometimes featuring Flecktarn, the German military's disruptive camouflage pattern.
Music
Characteristics

Musically, Keller Synth is distinguished from standard Dungeon Synth by its percussion and aggressive tone. It typically features cheap MIDI synthesizers mimicking medieval instruments like flutes and harpsichords played at high speeds, frequently layered with classic 1990s rave synthesizers like the Roland Alpha Juno to create buzzing, aggressive "Hoover" sounds. Vocals consist of high-pitched, pitch-shifted "goblin" voices or distorted shrieks buried in the mix. The genre relies on a deliberately "lo-fi" or "raw" production quality, mimicking the sound of music recorded on cheap cassette tapes in a basement.

The specific offshoot known as "Tänzelcore" places a much heavier emphasis on electronic music influences. Coined by Sigfrid and established around 2019 with Bergënot's Moselfrankian Tänzelcore Madness, Tänzelcore shifts away from Black Metal atmospheres to focus almost entirely on aggressive rhythmic elements. This variation heavily utilizes distorted kick drums derived from Hardcore Techno, Gabber, and Acid House, often incorporating "amen breaks" or four-on-the-floor patterns pushed to extreme clipping levels through analog mixer emulators or distortion pedals.

Criticism
Far-Right Symbolism and Dogwhistles

The Keller Synth scene has faced scrutiny regarding the political affiliations of prominent figures. The genre's pioneers, including Sigfrid and B.S.o.D., have been accused of using far-right imagery and dog whistles in their work. For instance, Andreas Bettinger's history includes direct documented ties to the German National Socialist Black Metal (NSBM) scene, including live performances with the prominent NSBM band Absurd. Critics note that the "Nose Thumb" gesture (🤥🤚🤚) has a history of use in antisemitic caricatures, though it is also a childish taunt in German-speaking countries. Concerns have also been raised regarding the prevalence of symbols like the number 88 in usernames associated with the scene.

The use of symbols such as the three-legged sun (Triskelion) has also sparked debate. While the symbol has ancient Celtic and Sicilian origins, it has occasionally been co-opted by fringe political movements. The community is divided between those who view the imagery as "edgy" internet irony and those who see it as a signal of far-right alignment.

In response to the far-right associations of the genre's founders, a counter-movement has emerged within the Red and Anarchist Black Metal (RABM) community. Independent labels like Grime Stone Records and various underground artists actively produce anti-fascist Keller Synth and Tänzelcore. These creators attempt to reclaim the chaotic DIY production style of the music to express anti-capitalist themes and subvert genre expectations, proving the sound itself is not inherently tied to the political extremism of its early pioneers.
Reception in the Dungeon Synth and Black Metal Scenes

Keller Synth and Tänzelcore frequently receive negative reception from the established Dungeon Synth and Black Metal communities. Many purists view the genre as an unserious offshoot lacking the atmosphere and musical rigor of traditional releases, often describing the style as relying entirely on shock value over substance. The scene is heavily criticized for its influx of younger audiences originating from TikTok and the SoundCloud Rap sphere, leading to accusations that the genre caters to internet trend-hoppers (such as fans of Yabujincore and Haunted Mound) rather than dedicated listeners.

The deliberate blending of abrasive dance beats, cheap synthesizer riffs, and intentionally poor production is frequently dismissed by detractors as an embarrassing mockery of the parent genres. Furthermore, the extreme edginess of the aesthetic, where artists are perceived to be roleplaying as drug addicts or leaning heavily into internet irony, frustrates traditionalists who view it as a superficial bastardization of black metal history rather than a legitimate musical evolution.

In response to these critiques, proponents of the genre argue that Tänzelcore is not intended to be a traditional subgenre of Black Metal. Instead, they argue that it is an electronic fusion where Black Metal is merely one textural element alongside high-energy dance influences. Many fans and artists point to the rhythmic structures of Hardcore Techno and Gabber as more accurate precursors to the Tänzelcore sound than conventional metal. This rave music lineage is visible in the discographies of the genre's founders, with Sigfrid utilizing projects like Carlos Esmeralda Jalapeño to directly incorporate the fast-paced melodies of Spanish Mákina into the scene.
